item.title: AI support agent in production
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Solo-built Azure platform for an AI support agent, live since 16 Oct 2026, for ~200 client organisations. A person reviews every note. Write actions require approval.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
This is a solo-built, Azure-hosted support agent that has been live since 16 October 2026 and is used across around 200 client organisations. When a new ticket arrives, the agent reads from the PSA, the documentation platform, the RMM, the EDR and the Microsoft 365 management tools, then writes an internal note with a diagnosis and a proposed next step; a person reviews that note, and anything that would change a customer environment runs only after approval. On the platform side the work is a read service and a separate execute service, each with its own identity and database role, secrets taken at runtime from Key Vault, PostgreSQL with Entra authentication, and a pipeline that tests every change, builds container images and deploys through Bicep.High-level flow of a new ticket. The agent reads those systems and writes an internal note for a person. Write actions require approval. Vendor names, network detail and client information are left out.
Platform
The platform is the work. The agent is the workload on top of it.
It is split into a read service and a separate execute service. Each has its own managed identity, its own Key Vault access and its own PostgreSQL role. The model has no credentials for customer systems. Write actions in a customer environment require approval. The approval path — mail, a confirmation page, a queue and a scheduled execute job — binds a decision to one unchanged proposal with a server-side token.
The services run on Azure Container Apps, with Azure Container Apps Jobs for scheduled work. Images are non-root and the build contains no secrets. Eighteen additive PostgreSQL migrations are applied by a migration tool that checks checksums, takes an advisory lock and uses a role per service. PostgreSQL uses Entra authentication over TLS.
Infrastructure is Bicep. The Azure DevOps pipeline has four stages: required pull-request tests with no Azure access, incremental image builds in Azure Container Registry, Container Apps deploys gated on a health check, then Bicep deployments that cannot roll an image backwards. An exclusive lock stops two releases from overlapping. Secrets are read from Key Vault at runtime through managed identity. Secret scanning runs in pre-commit and in CI, with a pinned tool version and a checksum, and dependency auditing runs on each build. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments API
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Spring Boot payments API with PostgreSQL 17. Multistage image, Compose, then local Kubernetes with a ConfigMap, a Secret and a Postgres volume.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
A small payments API for practising the path from code to a container to a cluster. The Java backend and the small frontend were scaffolded with Claude. The database, the containers and the Kubernetes setup are my own work. It runs on Minikube on my machine. The homelab deploy and AKS are still plans.
The steps, with the dates from the commits, are in theMini Payments build log.
What exists today
Accounts and transfers, with business-rule errors when a transfer is not allowed. Flyway appliesV1__create_accounts_and_transfers.sql on PostgreSQL 17.
A unit test for the transfer rules and an integration test for the transfer flow, run with the Maven wrapper.
Multistage Docker image. Disk usage went from 825 MB to 402 MB, content size from 265 MB to 128 MB. The process runs as a non-root user.
Docker Compose for the app and PostgreSQL, without a volume on the database.
Local Kubernetes, first on Docker Desktop, then Minikube. The app Deployment has 3 replicas. Postgres is one replica and is still a Deployment, not a StatefulSet.
Database URL and username in a ConfigMap. The password is in a Secret. The app reads both withenvFrom. Postgres reads the password withsecretKeyRef. The secret manifest is listed in.gitignore.
A 5Gi ReadWriteOnce PersistentVolumeClaim mounted at/var/lib/postgresql/data.
Planned, not built
StatefulSet for Postgres
Liveness and readiness probes
Resource requests and limits
Ingress
CI/CD to the homelab cluster, then AKS
Prometheus and Grafana ]]>

item.title: Monitoring Homelab
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Production-style Prometheus, Grafana and Alertmanager stack on a 3-node Proxmox cluster, paging through PagerDuty.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
A full monitoring and alerting pipeline on my 3-node Proxmox VE cluster. Every config file was written by hand, no helper scripts or one-click installers, so that I understand what each line does.Data flow from exporters to my phone.
What’s running
node_exporter on each Proxmox host, exposing CPU, memory, disk and network metrics.
Prometheus scraping every target every 15 seconds and evaluating the alert rules.
Grafana with a custom cluster-overview dashboard.
Alertmanager grouping alerts and routing them to PagerDuty.
blackbox_exporter probing the HTTP endpoints of the services I run.
Everything except node_exporter runs together in one LXC container; node_exporter runs directly on each host because it needs the host’s kernel data.
Alert rules
Seven rules, each with afor duration chosen so a short spike does not page me.
AlertFires whenForSeverity
NodeDownnode_exporter unreachable1 mincritical
DiskSpaceWarningroot partition above 85%5 minwarning
DiskSpaceCriticalroot partition above 95%2 mincritical
HighMemoryUsageRAM above 90%5 minwarning
HighCPUUsageCPU above 95%10 minwarning
EndpointDownHTTP probe fails2 mincritical
SlowResponseresponse slower than 5 s5 minwarningAll seven rules loaded and quiet.
DashboardsCustom cluster-overview dashboard in Grafana.
Paging
Alertmanager sends firing alerts to PagerDuty through the Events API. PagerDuty opens an incident and sends a text message; if I do not acknowledge it, it calls. From crash to phone buzz is about three minutes for most alerts: thefor duration plus Alertmanager’s grouping window.
I chose PagerDuty over Telegram or Discord because it is what companies use, and I wanted to set up real incident management: escalation policies, acknowledgements, on-call.A resolved test incident in PagerDuty.
The cluster underneath
Three second-hand small-form-factor PCs running Proxmox VE 9 as a cluster with high availability enabled. Storage is local on each node, with a ZFS pool onhost-1 for backups. Without shared storage an HA failover copies the container disk to another node, which takes minutes rather than seconds; fine for a homelab. All nodes are connected over a private overlay, with no ports exposed to the internet.The three nodes and what runs where. Hostnames in the source diagram are lab names.
What I learned
How Prometheus works under the hood: the pull model, scrape jobs, relabelling and PromQL.
Why Alertmanager is a separate component: grouping, routing and silencing are their own problem.
How companies handle incidents with PagerDuty: on-call, escalation and acknowledgement.
The install was the easy part. Understanding what each metric means, choosing thresholds that do not cry wolf, and building dashboards that actually help took most of the time. ]]>

item.title: Linux Security Hardening
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Two Bash scripts that bring a fresh Ubuntu/Debian server to a sensible baseline and audit the result.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
Two short Bash scripts: one hardens a freshly installed Ubuntu or Debian server, the other reports on the result. Tested on Ubuntu LTS.
Whatharden-server.sh does
Updates the system and enablesunattended-upgrades for automatic security patches.
Hardens SSH: no root login, no password authentication, port moved to 2222.
Configures UFW: default deny incoming, allow outgoing, open only 2222, 80 and 443.
Installs and enablesauditd for security event logging.
WhatSecurity-audit.sh reports
The active SSH settings forPort,PermitRootLogin andPasswordAuthentication.
UFW status and rules.
Failed SSH login attempts fromauth.log.
Packages with pending updates.
Audit output
sudo ./Security-audit.shLinux Security Audit SSH configuration:✓ Port 2222✓ PermitRootLogin no✓ PasswordAuthentication no UFW firewall status: Status: active Logging: on (low) Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), deny (routed) To Action From -- ------ ---- 2222/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere 80/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere 443/tcp ALLOW IN Anywhere Failed SSH login attempts (last 24h): sshd[2376]: Failed password for project from 10.0.0.50 port 30414 ssh2 sshd[4581]: Failed password for project from 10.0.0.50 port 30543 ssh2 Audit Complete
Why
I wrote these to practice Linux administration and server-side security hands-on. The scripts are short and readable on purpose: every line is something I can explain and defend.
What I’d do next
For one server, Bash is fine. For ten, this becomes an Ansible playbook with an inventory, and the audit becomes a set of[OK]/[FAIL] checks with an exit code so it can run from cron or CI. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: a volume for Postgres
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 10 November: a 5Gi ReadWriteOnce PersistentVolumeClaim at /var/lib/postgresql/data. The database is still a Deployment, not a StatefulSet.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
The same day as the ConfigMap, after that fight, I gave Postgres a disk. The commit is “PVC/PV fixed for database”.
k8s/database-pvc.yaml:
apiVersion:v1kind:PersistentVolumeClaimmetadata:name:database-pvcspec:resources:requests:storage:5GivolumeMode:FilesystemaccessModes:-ReadWriteOnce
The database Deployment mounts that claim at/var/lib/postgresql/data:
volumeMounts:-name:database-storagemountPath:/var/lib/postgresql/datavolumes:-name:database-storagepersistentVolumeClaim:claimName:database-pvc
The object is still a Deployment,replicas: 1. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a request for storage. It is not a StatefulSet. A StatefulSet is the controller that gives a stateful app a stable pod name and its own volume per pod. I do not have one.
On this commit I also addedk8s/app-secret.yaml to.gitignore.
What I’m learning next
Planned, not built.
StatefulSet. Stable pod name, own volume per pod. The claim above does not turn this Deployment into one, and raising the replica count still would not.
Liveness and readiness probes. Periodic checks. Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic. Liveness decides whether it is restarted.
Resource requests and limits. A request is what the scheduler reserves. A limit is the cap. Without a limit, one pod can use up the node. Without a request, the scheduler cannot place it properly.
Ingress. An HTTP router for the cluster, instead ofkubectl port-forward. A LoadBalancer or NodePort service per app does not scale.
CI/CD. Build the image and deploy it, first to the homelab cluster, then to AKS.
Prometheus and Grafana. Actuator with Micrometer collects HTTP requests, memory, threads and database connections. A dependency inpom.xml turns that into Prometheus text format, and the metrics endpoint has to be exposed. Grafana would be the dashboards. I test each step withkubectl describe,kubectl logs andkubectl get events. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: ConfigMap and Secret
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 9–10 November: database URL and username in a ConfigMap, the password in a Secret. One Secret with two expected key names, about two hours, then a 20-minute Flyway startup order.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
9 and 10 November were the ConfigMap and the Secret. A ConfigMap holds the non-secret settings, the database URL and the username, outside the Deployment and outside the image. The same image can then start with different values. The password goes in a Secret.
The app reads both withenvFrom:
envFrom:-configMapRef:name:mini-payments-config-secretRef:name:mini-payments-secrets
k8s/app-configmap.yaml:
apiVersion:v1kind:ConfigMapmetadata:name:mini-payments-configdata:SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL:"jdbc:postgresql://database:5432/payments"SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME:"payments"
The database Deployment no longer carries the password as a plain value. It reads one key from the same Secret:
-name:POSTGRES_PASSWORDvalueFrom:secretKeyRef:name:mini-payments-secretskey:SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD
The Secret manifest itself is not in this post.
What broke
This took about an hour and a half to two hours.
The YAML indentation was wrong. A field was a sibling when it needed to be a child, or the other way around.
kubectl describe on the pod shows where each environment variable comes from.
kubectl logs, and the output of a rollout, is where the error shows up. Mine wasunknown field "envFrom[0].name".name was sitting directly on theenvFrom entry. It belongs underconfigMapRef orsecretRef.
Those were symptoms. The design mistake under them was one Secret whose keys did not match what the two containers expected. The database wanted a different key name from the app, so the references did not line up. The wiring above is the fix: the app consumes the Secret as environment variables, and the database mapsPOSTGRES_PASSWORD to the keySPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD.
A note I wrote next to that, about how this usually works once it leaves a laptop: in production the database is typically outside the cluster, a managed service, with managed identity. Mini Payments is not that. The database pod is still in the cluster.
Flyway, 20 minutes
Starting the database while the app was already running left the app holding a connection to the old database, so the Flyway migration did not run. The database has to be up before the app, or come up with it. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: build log
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Index of the Mini Payments build log, from the 15 October plan to a Postgres volume on Minikube.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
I’m buildingMini Payments to practise the path a service takes: code, container, cluster. It’s a small payments API in Java 21 with Spring Boot and PostgreSQL. It has accounts, transfers between them, and business-rule errors when a transfer isn’t allowed.
I scaffolded the Java backend and the small frontend with Claude. My own work is the database, the containers and the Kubernetes setup. The commits below are onfeature/mini-payments-api-skeleton. It runs on Minikube on my machine. A homelab deploy and AKS are still plans.
The posts
15 Oct — Kickoff. The README states the plan.
24 Oct — App and PostgreSQL. The payments role was missing.
25 Oct — Images, Compose, database manifests. 825 MB disk down to 402 MB.
26 Oct — Docker Desktop Kubernetes. Three app replicas, one database replica.
3 Nov — Minikube. The cluster could not see the host image.
9–10 Nov — ConfigMap and Secret. One Secret, two expected key names.
10 Nov — A volume for Postgres. A PersistentVolumeClaim on a Deployment.
Where it stands
The app Deployment has 3 replicas ofmini-payments-api:dev. Postgres 17 is one replica, still a Deployment, with a 5Gi ReadWriteOnce claim mounted at/var/lib/postgresql/data. The database URL and username come from a ConfigMap. The password comes from a Secret. I reach the API withkubectl port-forward.
What I’m learning next
Planned, not built. These are the notes I wrote for the steps after the volume.
StatefulSet. A StatefulSet is the controller for a stateful app: a stable pod name, and its own volume per pod. The volume I have does not make the database Deployment a StatefulSet. Raisingreplicas is not how you make Postgres reliable.
Liveness and readiness probes. Kubernetes checks the container on a schedule. Readiness decides whether traffic may go to the pod. Liveness decides whether the pod should be restarted.
Resource requests and limits. A request is what the scheduler reserves. A limit is the cap on the machine. Without a limit, one pod can use up the node. Without a request, the scheduler cannot place the pod properly.
Ingress. An HTTP router into the cluster, in place of port-forward. A LoadBalancer or NodePort service per app does not scale. Ingress is the one front door.
CI/CD. A pipeline that builds the image and deploys it, first to my homelab cluster, then to AKS.
Prometheus and Grafana. Spring Boot Actuator, with the Micrometer that is already there, collects HTTP requests, memory, threads and database connections. A dependency inpom.xml turns those metrics into the text format Prometheus reads. The endpoint still has to be opened: Spring Boot only exposes health over HTTP until then. Grafana is the dashboard in front of that. I check each of these steps withkubectl describe,kubectl logs andkubectl get events. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: Minikube can't see the image
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 3 November: moved to Minikube. The app pods stayed down until minikube image load, then port-forward again.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
On 3 November I moved the same manifests from Docker Desktop’s cluster to Minikube. The app containers would not start. Minikube does not see an image I built on the host until that image is loaded into the cluster.
Build on the host, then load the tag the Deployment already uses:
docker build -t mini-payments-api:dev .minikube image load mini-payments-api:dev
The Service is still only inside the cluster, so the port-forward is the way onto it:
kubectl port-forward svc/app 8080:8080]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: the API on Docker Desktop Kubernetes
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 26 October: the app Deployment at 3 replicas and a Service, on Docker Desktop. Postgres cut from 3 replicas to 1.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
On 26 October I added the app manifests and ran them on the Kubernetes cluster built into Docker Desktop.
k8s/app-deployment.yaml runs 3 replicas ofmini-payments-api:dev. The container listens on 8080. The datasource URL, username and password are environment variables on the pod. The URL isjdbc:postgresql://database:5432/payments and the username ispayments. The password is set the same way. I’m not printing the value.
k8s/app-service.yaml is namedapp. It selects those pods and exposes port 8080. Traffic to the Service is spread across the three replicas.
One database replica
The database Deployment from 25 October asked for 3 replicas. I set it to 1.
Postgres here has no shared disk. Each pod has its own data directory. The Service spreads requests across the pods: the app creates an account through one pod, reads it through another, and gets “not found”. A database is stateful. Adding replicas does not make it reliable. That takes a stable identity per pod and a volume per pod, which is a StatefulSet and a PersistentVolumeClaim. On 26 October I have neither, so the database stays at one replica.
Reaching it
The Services are only inside the cluster. From the laptop:
kubectl port-forward svc/app 8080:8080
To look at the tables, exec into the Postgres pod. The pod I used that day:
kubectlexec -it database-79d5d77c8b-d8lv9 -- psql -U payments -d payments]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: images, Compose, and the database manifests
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 25 October: a single-stage image, then a multistage image at half the size, Compose without a volume, and the first database manifests.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
25 October was four commits: a single-stage image, a multistage Dockerfile, Compose, and the first Kubernetes manifests, which were only for the database.
Single-stage image
The first image wrapped a JAR I had built by hand.
./mvnw package -DskipTests
docker build -t mini-payments-api:dev . —-t is the name and tag, and the. is the build context.
Run it, with the database settings as environment variables.-e sets a variable,--rm removes the container when it stops, and-p 8080:8080 publishes the port. The app reaches Postgres on the host throughhost.docker.internal. The password is one of those variables. I’m not printing it.
Anyone who wanted to run that image had to compile first, and the image was large.
Multistage Dockerfile
docker build now compiles and packages. The final stage is the image. This is the Dockerfile:
# stage 1: Building image containing both Maven and Java 21FROMmaven:3.9.9-eclipse-temurin-21asBUILDWORKDIR/appCOPY . .RUN mvn package -DskipTests# stage 2: runtimeFROMeclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpineasRUNTIMEWORKDIR/appRUN adduser -S appuserCOPY --from=BUILD /app/target/*-SNAPSHOT.jar app.jarUSERappuserEXPOSE8080ENTRYPOINT["java","-jar","app.jar"]
Stage 1 is the Maven image with a JDK 21, andas BUILD is the name the next stage copies from.COPY . . copies the whole project. That is a weak layer: a source change and a dependency change bust the same cache. Copyingpom.xml first and resolving dependencies in their own layer is the next improvement. For now it is fine.
Stage 2 is a JRE on Alpine, so the runtime image stays small.adduser -S appuser is Alpine’s command, not the one from the Maven image.USER appuser is who the process runs as.EXPOSE 8080 is documentation. The entrypoint isjava -jar app.jar.
ImageDisk usageContent size
Single-stage (test:tag1)825 MB265 MB
Multistage (mini-payments-api:dev)402 MB128 MB
A smaller image means faster pulls on a cluster, faster scale-up and a lighter pipeline.
Compose
docker-compose.yml starts PostgreSQL 17 next to the app. The app service usesbuild: ., so Compose builds the Dockerfile and starts the container.depends_on waits for the database service. There is no volume on the database: a restart drops the data. The environment variables for both services have to be in the file. I’m not pasting it here, because it contains the database password.
Database manifests
The same evening I addedk8s/database-deployment.yaml andk8s/database-service.yaml. The Deployment runspostgres:17. The Service is nameddatabase, port 5432, and that name is what the app will connect to.
That first Deployment setreplicas: 3, and it put the database name, user and password in the pod environment. The password value stays out of this post. The next day I changed the replica count. A Service in front of three Postgres pods that do not share a disk is the problem the next post is about. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: app and PostgreSQL
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 24 October: Claude scaffolded the Java and the frontend. PostgreSQL 17 is my work, including the missing payments role.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
The commit on 24 October is the base build. The message on it is blunt: the backend and the frontend were built by Claude, and I made the PostgreSQL database myself. That split is the point. I am practising the platform side.
The API is Java 21 and Spring Boot. It has accounts, transfers between them, and business-rule errors when a transfer is not allowed. Flyway appliesV1__create_accounts_and_transfers.sql, so the schema is built the same way every time. The database is PostgreSQL 17.
./mvnw test runs the tests../mvnw spring-boot:run starts the app, and it will not stay up without the database.
The payments role
The first database container did not create thepayments role, so Postgres never became usable and Spring Boot, which waits on it, did not start either. I had passedPOSTGRES_USERS instead ofPOSTGRES_USER. The image does not invent that role. It creates the role fromPOSTGRES_USER.
I removed the container and created it again withPOSTGRES_USER,POSTGRES_PASSWORD andPOSTGRES_DB set, plus a named volume (payments-data mounted at/var/lib/postgresql/data) so the data survives a restart. I’m not putting the password in this post. The database name and the role are bothpayments.
From the host, with the app in a second terminal:
SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/payments\SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=payments\./mvnw spring-boot:run
And into the database:
psql -h localhost -U payments -d payments
The commands I actually use inpsql:
CommandWhat it does
\conninfoWhich database and user am I connected as?
\dtList the tables
\d accountsColumns, constraints and indexes of a table
\diList the indexes
\xToggle expanded rows
\qQuit
When the app fails to start, check the dependency it is waiting on before debugging the app. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: kickoff
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 15 October: the repo and the README plan. A Spring Boot API, PostgreSQL, a Dockerfile, then CI/CD to the homelab.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
On 15 October I createdmini-payments-api. The README is the plan, written as preparation for an internship.
The plan is a payments API on Java and Spring Boot, a PostgreSQL database, a Dockerfile, and a CI/CD pipeline that deploys to my own Kubernetes cluster on the homelab. Monitoring would be Prometheus and Grafana.
That is the plan. The pipeline, the deploy onto the homelab cluster, and the monitoring are still plans. The posts after this one are the parts that are built. ]]>

item.title: Building a monitoring stack from scratch
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Notes on setting up Prometheus + Alertmanager + PagerDuty by hand on my home cluster.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
I wanted monitoring on my home cluster, so I set up Prometheus, Alertmanager and PagerDuty step by step. Writing the configs myself instead of using a pre-made stack helped me understand what each part actually does. These are my notes.
The setup
Three Proxmox nodes. Each host runsnode_exporter directly, because it needs the host’s kernel data. Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana andblackbox_exporter run together in one LXC container.
Prometheus scrapes every 15 seconds. The two jobs that matter:
scrape_configs:-job_name:'proxmox-nodes'static_configs:-targets:-'10.0.0.11:9100'# host-1-'10.0.0.12:9100'# host-2-'10.0.0.13:9100'# host-3-job_name:'blackbox-http'metrics_path:/probeparams:module:[http_2xx]static_configs:-targets:-'http://10.0.0.20:81'# reverse proxy-'http://10.0.0.21/admin'# DNS admin-'http://localhost:3000'# Grafanarelabel_configs:-source_labels:[__address__]target_label:__param_target-source_labels:[__param_target]target_label:instance-target_label:__address__replacement:localhost:9115
Theblackbox-http relabel block took me a while to get right. The__param_target rewrite is what tellsblackbox_exporter which URL to probe on each scrape — without it, you get metrics but the target is empty.
Alert rules
Seven rules, each with afor duration so a short spike doesn’t page me:
NodeDown — node_exporter unreachable for 1 minute
DiskSpaceWarning — root partition above 85% for 5 minutes
DiskSpaceCritical — above 95% for 2 minutes
HighMemoryUsage — RAM above 90% for 5 minutes
HighCPUUsage — CPU above 95% for 10 minutes
EndpointDown — HTTP probe failing for 2 minutes
SlowResponse — response slower than 5 seconds for 5 minutes
Alertmanager
The mental model that helped me: labels are inputs, routes are filters, receivers are destinations.
route:receiver:'default-pagerduty'group_by:['alertname','instance']group_wait:30sgroup_interval:5mrepeat_interval:4hroutes:-matchers:-severity = "info"receiver:'null'receivers:-name:'default-pagerduty'pagerduty_configs:-routing_key:'...'-name:'null'
Info-level alerts go to a null receiver. Everything else pages.
Testing the chain
I needed to verify alerts actually reach PagerDuty without breaking a real service. I added aTestAlert rule with a constant true expression:
-alert:TestAlertexpr:vector(1) > 0for:0mlabels:severity:criticalannotations:summary:"Manual test alert"
Reload Prometheus, wait for the alert to fire, get the text message. A few minutes later the phone call came in because I didn’t acknowledge it. Then I disabled the rule again.
Things that tripped me up
A wrong__param_target rewrite meant every blackbox metric had an emptyinstance label, so Alertmanager couldn’t deduplicate alerts.
group_interval: 30s (which I had early on) flooded my phone with 12 pages from one outage.5m is much saner.
I had the wrong PagerDuty integration key for a few days. Alerts fired in Alertmanager but PagerDuty showed nothing. The Alertmanager logs surfaced it eventually.
Repo
github.com/E-mma9/Monitoring-Homelab — full config and Grafana dashboard JSON. ]]>

item.title: Hardening Ubuntu with Bash
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Two scripts for taking a fresh Ubuntu/Debian box to a defensible baseline.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
I wrote two Bash scripts to harden a fresh Ubuntu/Debian server and audit it afterwards. Posting the structure and a few notes here.
What gets configured
harden-server.sh:
System updates, withunattended-upgrades enabled for security patches
SSH — disable root login, disable password auth, move to port 2222
UFW — default-deny incoming, allow 2222/80/443
auditd installed and enabled for security logging
Security-audit.sh:
Prints the active SSH settings forPort,PermitRootLogin andPasswordAuthentication
Shows UFW status and rules
Lists failed SSH logins fromauth.log
Lists packages with pending updates
Keeping it simple
The SSH changes are threesed one-liners:
sed -i's/^#\?PermitRootLogin .*/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_configsed -i's/^#\?PasswordAuthentication .*/PasswordAuthentication no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_configsed -i's/^#\?Port .*/Port 2222/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
The^#\? matches both the commented default and an existing value, so the line gets replaced either way.ufw skips rules that already exist. Together that makes the script safe to re-run.
The audit script
The audit is deliberately plain: show the state, let a human read it.
grep -E'^(Port|PermitRootLogin|PasswordAuthentication)' /etc/ssh/sshd_configufw status verbosegrep"Failed password" /var/log/auth.log| tail -20apt list --upgradable
The next step is turning each line into an[OK]/[FAIL] check with an exit code, so it can run from cron or CI and fail loudly on drift.
When this stops being the right tool
For one server, Bash is fine. For ten, I’d move to Ansible — the inventory and playbook structure pay for themselves. The scripts were a way to get familiar with the actual files and directives. After that, config management makes more sense.

github.com/E-mma9/Linux-Security-Hardening ]]>

item.title: Notes on my 3-node Proxmox cluster
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Hardware, networking, and what I've learned running three nodes at home.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
A short write-up on my home Proxmox cluster — why three nodes, how it’s wired, and what I’ve learned. I get asked about this a lot, so this is the canonical answer.
Hardware
Three second-hand small-form-factor PCs, a Dell OptiPlex and two HP ProDesks, all on Intel i5 CPUs:
host-1 — 16 GB RAM, 238 GB NVMe for the OS, plus a 931 GB HDD as a ZFS pool for backups
host-2 — 8 GB RAM, 119 GB NVMe
host-3 — 8 GB RAM, 119 GB SSD
All three run Proxmox VE 9, headless, joined in one cluster with high availability enabled.
Why three instead of one
A single bigger server would be cheaper to run and quieter. Three nodes give me things a single host can’t:
Quorum — three is the minimum for the cluster to keep making decisions when one node drops out. With two, losing one locks the cluster up.
HA — Proxmox restarts a failed service up to three times on the same node, then migrates it to another one. I can take a node down for kernel updates without losing the services on it.
Live migration —pct migrate andqm migrate move a workload between hosts with a few seconds of network blip. Useful operationally, and useful for testing.
Real failure modes — pulling a power cable on one node behaves differently from rebooting a single host. The behaviour during recovery is the actual reason I have three.
Networking
Everything sits on one bridged LAN viavmbr0, not segmented yet. Remote access goes over Tailscale, so nothing is exposed to the internet: no port forwards, no public IPs on the nodes.
Storage
Storage is local on each node. There is no shared storage: a distributed storage layer would need an extra disk per node, and I did not want to spend on that yet. The ZFS pool onhost-1 holds the backups for the whole cluster.
The trade-off shows up on failover. Without shared storage, HA has to copy the container disk to the target node before it can start there, so a failover takes minutes rather than seconds. For a homelab that’s fine.
What it’s not
Not cheaper than a single server, on hardware or electricity
Not quieter — three fans humming
Not simpler
It’s just closer to a production setup, which is the only reason I run it.
What I’d do differently
Shared storage first. An extra disk per node for distributed storage, or an NFS share, would turn failover from minutes into seconds. Network segmentation is next on the list. ]]>
